content: CDON, also known as Cell adhesion molecule-related/down-regulated by oncogenes, is a transmembrane glycoprotein that belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily of cell adhesion molecules. It is a conserved protein that plays a critical role in various developmental processes. CDON and its related protein, BOC, are cell surface receptors that belong to the immunoglobulin (Ig)/fibronectin type III (FNIII) repeat family. These proteins are involved in myogenic differentiation, a process essential for muscle development. During development, CDON and BOC are coexpressed and form complexes with each other in a cis configuration. While their ectodomains are structurally related, each protein has a distinct and unique long cytoplasmic tail. CDON is highly expressed in specific regions during embryonic development, such as the somites and the dorsal lips of the neural tube in embryonic day 8.5 mice. It is also expressed in both proliferating and differentiating myoblast cell lines, where it mediates critical cell–cell interactions between muscle precursor cells, which are essential for myogenesis. Additionally, CDON is expressed in neural crest precursor cells, where it regulates the localization of N-cadherin, a mechanism that facilitates directed migration of neural crest cells. The CDON protein has been shown to bind to all three mammalian isoforms of hedgehog proteins: Sonic Hedgehog (Shh), Indian Hedgehog (Ihh), and Desert Hedgehog (Dhh). Mutations in the CDON gene have significant clinical implications. These mutations are believed to reduce the activity of the Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway, which is crucial for cell proliferation, differentiation, and tissue patterning during various stages of development. CDON has been implicated in the differentiation of midbrain dopaminergic neurons through its interaction with the Shh signaling pathway. Mutations in the CDON gene have been associated with holoprosencephaly, a severe structural brain anomaly in which the developing forebrain fails to properly separate into the right and left hemispheres. Gene knockdown studies have provided additional insights into the role of CDON. In zebrafish, CDON knockdown using morpholinos disrupted eye development. In chick embryos, CDON was found to be essential for regulating the size of the optic stalk and the ventral retina. Double CDON knockout mice exhibited optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH), a hallmark feature of septo-optic dysplasia (SOD). Interestingly, a similar phenotype was observed in mice exposed prenatally to ethanol. CDON−/− mice also displayed cardiac dysfunction characterized by increased fibrosis, which was mediated through hyperactivation of the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway. CDON has been shown to interact with other proteins, including CDH1 (E-cadherin) and BOC, further highlighting its role in cellular signaling and developmental processes.
